sections.body: Citation mapping and discovery is the part of AI research that treats the scholarly record as a network rather than a pile of PDFs. Artificial intelligence reads titles, abstracts, full texts, and reference lists to build citation graphs, then uses embeddings and language models to group papers by meaning instead of by keyword. In practice this means a system can show which earlier work a new paper builds on, which later work corrects or extends it, and which papers sit between fields. It can also classify how a citation is used, for example as background, method, or contrast, rather than treating every reference as a simple vote. The work is not just search, it is structure, provenance, and discovery across a literature that grows faster than any person can read. This site's library of 288 research papers and 13,608 extracted claims gives a concrete place to see those structures at a small scale.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts of this field are mature, especially basic citation extraction, deduplication, and graph construction from clean metadata. Clustering by meaning works well enough to surface related papers, but it still struggles with ambiguous terms, preprint versions, and fields that use the same words for different ideas. Citation intent classification is useful but imperfect, because a reference can serve several purposes at once and authors rarely state them plainly. Bridge studies are harder to detect automatically, since a paper that connects two fields may look marginal in both. Trend forecasting is the least settled area, because citation counts lag real shifts by years and early signals are noisy. The honest limit is that these tools can map and suggest, but they cannot yet replace expert judgment about why a line of work matters.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: Each page in this section takes one piece of that larger map. Citation Graphs Over Time shows how the network grows and shifts, which is the page to read for historical structure and for seeing how a field accumulates references. Clustering Papers by Meaning explains how AI groups papers by content rather than by citation links, which is the page for finding related work that does not cite each other. How a Paper Is Cited focuses on the local context of a single reference, which is the page for understanding whether a citation supports, disputes, or merely mentions a claim. Bridge Studies Between Fields looks at papers that connect separate research communities, which is the page for interdisciplinary discovery and for finding work that sits between two literatures. Forecasting Research Trends turns those structures into forward looking signals, which is the page for thinking about where attention may move next, with the caveat that forecasts are probabilistic and often wrong.
